title: Steamed salmon and vegetables
skill: Steaming fish and vegetables in a basket

notes.text: Steam the salmon in two batches, and keep the first batch on the platter under foil.

move.title: Densest first, fish last
move.body: Steaming cooks food in the hot, wet air above boiling water. Nothing browns, so the vegetables keep their color and the salmon stays moist. Today you'll set up a steamer basket, steam potatoes, carrots, and green beans in order from slowest to quickest so each is crisp-tender, then steam the salmon on its own to 145°F, with a cold lemon-dill yogurt sauce made first.

why.title: How steam cooks
why.body: Boiling water makes steam at about 212°F. When the steam touches cooler food, it turns back into water and gives up its heat all at once, so steam cooks faster than dry air at the same temperature. Because it never gets hotter than about 212°F, nothing browns or burns.

why.title: Water below the basket
why.body: The food sits above the water, not in it. If the water touches the basket, the bottom layer boils instead of steaming and turns soft and pale. An inch of water lasts about 20 minutes at a steady boil, so check it halfway.

why.title: Densest first
why.body: Potatoes are dense and take about 12 minutes; carrot coins take about 6; green beans take about 4. Adding them in that order means they're all done at the same moment.

why.title: Crisp-tender
why.body: A crisp-tender vegetable is bright, and a knife goes in with a little push at the center. Steamed past that, green vegetables turn olive-gray and soft, because their color breaks down with long heat.

why.title: Lift the lid away from you
why.body: A cloud of 212°F steam comes out when the lid lifts, and steam burns faster than boiling water. Lift the far edge first, so the lid is a shield between you and the steam.

why.title: 145°F, and it flakes
why.body: Salmon is done when the thickest part reads 145°F and it separates into flakes when pressed with a fork. White beads on the surface mean it's starting to overcook; take it off now.

wrong.fix: Turn off the burner, let the pot cool a minute, and pour in more hot water from the kettle or a measuring cup. Next time, check the water level when the potatoes come out.

wrong.sign: The green beans are olive-gray and soft
wrong.fix: They steamed too long. They still taste fine; next time pull them at 4 minutes and test.

wrong.sign: The potatoes are still hard in the middle
wrong.fix: Put them back in the basket and steam 3 more minutes. Cut them the same size next time so they cook evenly.

wrong.sign: There are white beads all over the salmon
wrong.fix: That's protein pushed out by overcooking. It's safe; spoon the sauce over it. Next time, start checking 2 minutes sooner.

quiz.q: Why do the potatoes go in the steamer first?
choices: They're densest and take the longest
quiz.explain: Densest first, so everything finishes together.

choices: Below the basket, not touching it
Up to the middle of the food
quiz.explain: Food in the water boils instead of steaming.

quiz.q: How do you lift the lid off a steaming pot?
choices: Far edge first, so the lid shields you
quiz.explain: Steam burns faster than boiling water.

choices: 145°F in the thickest part, and it flakes
quiz.explain: The same check as baked salmon.

substitutions.note: Thinner cod pieces may be done in 6 minutes.
Stir the lemon, dill, and garlic into mayonnaise instead.

steps.text: Grate the lemon's zest on the fine side of the box grater into the small bowl, then cut the lemon in half and squeeze in the juice of one half. Mince the garlic fine. Stir the yogurt, zest, lemon juice, dill, garlic, and the sauce's salt together. Cover it and put it in the fridge.
steps.tip: Cut the other lemon half into 4 wedges for the table.

steps.text: Cut the potatoes into 1-inch pieces: halve the small ones and quarter the big ones, so every piece is about the same size.
Peel the carrots and cut them on a slight angle into coins ¼ inch thick. Snap or cut the stem ends off the green beans.

Open the steamer basket in the large pot. Pour the pot's water in around it: it should come up to just below the basket, not through the holes. Put the lid on and bring the water to a boil over high heat.
With oven mitts, lift the lid, far edge first. Spread the potatoes in the basket, put the lid back on, and turn the heat to medium-high so it keeps a steady boil.
steps.tip: You'll hear a steady rattle of boiling water. If it goes quiet, the heat is too low or the water's gone.

steps.text: Lift the lid, far edge first, and scatter the carrots over the potatoes. Lid on.
Lift the lid, far edge first, and lay the green beans on top. Lid on.
Lift the lid away from you and test the biggest potato and a carrot with the paring knife. Both should take the knife with a little push at the center. If not, steam 2 more minutes.
steps.look: Bright orange carrots, bright green beans, and a knife slides into the potatoes with a little push.

steps.text: With the tongs, move the vegetables to the plate, sprinkle them with a pinch of salt, and cover them with foil. Check the water: if it's under half an inch, add 1 more cup and let it boil again.
Smell the salmon: it should smell clean, not fishy. Pat it dry with paper towels and season both sides with the salmon's salt and pepper.
Throw the paper towels and the salmon's package away, and wash your hands with soap.
Lift the lid, far edge first. Lay the salmon in the basket in one layer with space between the pieces, using the spatula. Lid on.

Turn off the burner. Lift the lid away from you and slide the thermometer into the side of the thickest piece. It needs to read 145°F and flake when you press it with the fork. If not, put the lid back on and steam 2 more minutes with the heat on.
Lift the salmon out with the spatula and set it on the vegetables. Spoon the olive oil over everything and serve with the cold sauce and the lemon wedges.
